sections.title: Policy and access to the centre
sections.text:
Lille has tightened on-street parking in steps and runs it directly. The 2018 national reform turned paid street parking into a user fee and replaced the national €17 fine with a post-parking charge that each local authority sets. Lille runs the system itself, where Roubaix delegated it to a semi-public company [0]. In September 2022 the council adopted a plan to extend paid street parking progressively, up to 2025, to almost the whole city, to clear public space of long-stay 'ventouse' cars and improve turnover [1]. A new tariff grid took effect in April 2023 with higher prices everywhere, and the charge for not paying rose from €17 to €35 in the centre and €25 elsewhere [3]. Zones now run from an orange hypercentre, with 30 minutes free and no resident parking, out to green residential districts, and resident subscriptions have three income-based levels, €10, €15 and €25 [4][5].

The metropolitan plans point the same way. The Métropole Européenne de Lille adopted its mobility plan to 2035 in October 2023, treating parking as a central tool [7][8]. It recommends ceilings on parking in new offices, lower minimum norms for housing near good transport and more park-and-ride upstream of dense areas, and the PLU3 land-use plan of June 2024 turns this into rules, including a hyper-central Lille sector [8]. The low-emission zone, in force across all 95 communes since January 2025, bans only the oldest, unclassified vehicles [9][10]. Parliament voted in April 2026 to abolish such zones, but the Constitutional Council struck the provision down in May as a legislative rider, leaving the framework in place [11][12].

The centre itself has been closing to cars. The Grand'Place became fully pedestrian on 12 January 2026. The roughly 300-space underground car park beneath it stays open via rue Nationale, and the city points to about ten car parks within a 10-minute walk [13]. For the Braderie in September 2026 central access was banned from Friday evening, the city-centre car parks closed and 13 park-and-ride sites were offered [15].

sections.title: Parking developments
sections.text:
The metropolis counted 19,561 spaces in its city-centre car parks and 5,526 in park-and-ride sites, among 47 access-controlled car parks open to the public [17]. Most are owned by the Métropole, with Lille owning the Grand'Place and Vieux-Lille car parks. The city-centre car parks are run under concessions by Indigo, Effia or a semi-public company, and the park-and-ride sites by Ilévia [18]. The Saint-Philibert park-and-ride in Lomme is being rebuilt and extended from 335 to about 570 spaces [24]. Between 1998 and 2016 the metropolitan car fleet grew by 16%, and where parking is restricted or priced the car share falls by nearly 20 points in areas served by tram or metro [16].

Prices are high compared with nearby towns. A 2023 comparison found Lille's car parks cost on average 1.5 times those of Roubaix and Tourcoing from the first half hour, and twice as much from one hour, with an average monthly subscription of €134 against €40 and €44 [19]. Charging is being added through the metropolitan Iléwatt service, which is to reach nearly 900 points at nearly 300 locations, and in 25 public car parks whose operators set their own prices [25]. A 2021 strategy aimed at more than 4,000 public points within four years, from 400 [26]. A local opposition group has claimed that the city's concessions for the Grand'Place and Vieux-Lille car parks run to 2049 and 2054; this is a claim, not an official figure [20]. We found no sourced figures on a shift from the centre to shopping centres.

sections.title: Operators, positioning and utilisation
sections.text:
Our Lille data cover eleven car parks with 7,127 spaces, all within 1 km of the Grand'Place: five within 500 m (2,319 spaces) and six between 500 m and 1 km (4,808), including the 2,873-space Euralille shopping-centre car park. Indigo runs six of them (5,060 spaces) and Effia four (1,767), with prices close to each other. Indigo's median is €2.55 an hour and Effia's €2.25. In 2023 Effia's République, Opéra and Nouveau Siècle were the cheapest of the public car parks, and Euralille's Gare A and B the dearest for long stays [19]. The operators' own pages on 7 October 2026 show slightly higher hourly prices than our stored figures, for example €2.10 an hour at Nouveau Siècle against €1.80 in our data, and €3.20 an hour at Tanneurs against €2.50 [22][23].

Occupancy over August to early October 2026 averaged 54% on weekdays and 52% at weekends. The fullest is the Lille Flandres station car park, run by Effia (374 spaces, 85% on weekdays and 83% at weekends, €2.75 an hour), followed by Plaza (323 spaces, 81%) and Euralille Gare B (160 spaces, 66%). The Euralille shopping-centre car park is 55% full. The quietest are Rihour-Printemps (300 spaces, 17%), whose operator is not stated, and Euralille Gare C (541 spaces, 23%). Within 500 m of the Grand'Place the average is 51%, against 55% for the car parks 500 m to 1 km away.

Price does not decide occupancy: Lille Flandres is Effia's dearest car park and its fullest. Effia's three city-centre car parks are busier at weekends than on weekdays (Opéra 73%, against 54%), while Euralille Gare A drops from 59% to 33%. The data cover the summer holidays, so term-time figures may differ, and we have no multi-year history for Lille.
